claim: Bacteria inhibit and kill one another with a diverse array of compounds, including bacteriocins and antibiotics.
source: Bacteria inhibit and kill one another with a diverse array of compounds, including bacteriocins and antibiotics.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature on bacterial competition, as evidenced by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Regulated strategies that use quorum sensing or stress responses to regulate toxin production will readily evolve as they outcompete constitutive toxin production.
source: Our model predicts that regulated strategies, which use quorum sensing or stress responses to regulate toxin production, will readily evolve as they outcompete constitutive toxin production.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 2 and discussed in the Results section.

claim: A particularly successful strategy is to upregulate toxin production in response to an incoming competitor's toxin, which can be achieved via stress responses that detect cell damage (competition sensing).
source: Amongst regulated strategies, we show that a particularly successful strategy is to upregulate toxin production in response to an incoming competitor's toxin, which can be achieved via stress responses that detect cell damage (competition sensing).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4, where toxin-sensing strategies outperform other regulatory strategies.

claim: Reciprocation in bacteria serves not to promote peaceful outcomes but to enable efficient and effective attacks.
source: However, in contrast to classical results, we argue that reciprocation in bacteria serves not to promote peaceful outcomes but to enable efficient and effective attacks.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and interpretation presented in the manuscript, particularly in the discussion of coevolution of regulated attack strategies.

claim: Bacteria commonly live in dense and diverse communities where competition for space and nutrients can be intense.
source: Bacteria commonly live in dense and diverse communities where competition for space and nutrients can be intense (Kim et al., 2014; Hibbing et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria have evolved a wide range of competitive traits including contact-dependent inhibition, the type VI secretion system, narrow-spectrum bacteriocins, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
source: As a response to such ecology, bacteria have evolved a wide range of competitive traits (Granato et al., 2019), including contact-dependent inhibition (Ghequire and De Mot, 2014; Hayes et al., 2010; Aoki et al., 2010), the type VI secretion system (Miyata et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2014; Hood et al., 2010), narrow-spectrum bacteriocins, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (Bérdy, 2005; Riley and Wertz, 2002; Chao and Levin, 1981), which can kill or inhibit other strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteriocidal toxins are found in almost all major bacterial lineages.
source: Bacteriocidal toxins are found in almost all major bacterial lineages (Riley and Wertz, 2002; Granato et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Single species commonly make use of multiple toxins and diverse means of attack.
source: and single species commonly make use of multiple toxins and diverse means of attack (Granato et al., 2019; Be'er et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012; Steele et al., 2017; Jamet and Nassif, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxin production can prevent competing strains from invading a niche.
source: This toxin-based warfare is also important for bacterial ecology and evolution, with evidence that toxin production can prevent competing strains from invading a niche (Sassone-Corsi et al., 2016; Nakatsuji et al., 2017; Zipperer et al., 2016; O'Sullivan et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxin production can kill off coexisting strains.
source: kill off coexisting strains (Granato et al., 2019; Majeed et al., 2011; Speare et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxin production can help strains to invade new niches.
source: or help strains to invade new niches (Kommineni et al., 2015; Wiener, 1996; Sana et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxin production is often tightly regulated.
source: This work has revealed that toxin production is often tightly regulated (Miyata et al., 2013; Anderson et al., 2012; Ghazaryan et al., 2014; Bernard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are many new antibiotics that remain undetected because they are only activated under certain conditions.
source: Indeed, it is thought that there are many new antibiotics that remain undetected because they are only activated under certain conditions (Maldonado et al., 2003; Abrudan et al., 2015; Traxler et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A major form of regulation in bacteria is quorum sensing whereby cells secrete a small molecule and respond to it dependent upon its concentration.
source: A major form of regulation in bacteria is quorum sensing (Fuqua et al., 1994; Navarro et al., 2008; Eickhoff and Bassler, 2018) whereby cells secrete a small molecule and respond to it dependent upon its concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge about bacterial quorum sensing.

claim: Some antibiotics and bacteriocins are regulated by quorum sensing, which is thought to ensure that toxin production occurs at the right cell density.
source: Some antibiotics and bacteriocins are regulated by quorum sensing, which is thought to ensure that toxin production occurs at the right cell density (Hibbing et al., 2010; Chandler et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria engage in 'competition sensing' whereby they use nutrient stress and cell damage to detect ecological competition.
source: This led to the argument that, in addition to quorum sensing, bacteria engage in 'competition sensing' whereby they use nutrient stress and cell damage to detect ecological competition (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Lories et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Factors such as strain frequency, nutrient level, the level of strain mixing (relatedness), and the cost of toxin production are all important for whether bacteria employ toxins.
source: This work has highlighted that factors such as strain frequency, nutrient level, the level of strain mixing (relatedness), and the cost of toxin production are all important for whether bacteria employ toxins at all (Bucci et al., 2011; Gardner et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2006; Gordon and Riley, 1999; Frank, 1994; Levin, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical literature.

claim: Natural selection for warfare can have consequences for the evolution of diversity.
source: Other models have highlighted how natural selection for warfare can have consequences for the evolution of diversity (Frank, 1994; Biernaskie et al., 2013; Kelsic et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2017), including via rock-paper-scissor dynamics between different genotypes (Czárán et al., 2002; Kerr et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical literature.

claim: All three types of regulated strategies (nutrient sensing, quorum sensing, and toxin sensing) carry benefits relative to non-regulated production.
source: We find that all three types of regulated strategies carry benefits relative to non-regulated production
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in Figure 2.

claim: For short-lived resources, the three types of regulation offer largely equivalent alternatives for controlling attacks.
source: and, for short-lived resources, the three types of regulation offer largely equivalent alternatives for controlling attacks.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3b and Appendix 1—figure 10.

claim: For long-lived environments, responding to incoming attacks is often the best performing strategy.
source: However, for long-lived environments, responding to incoming attacks is often the best performing strategy.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: A key benefit to reciprocation in long-lived environments is the ability to downregulate a toxin once a competitor is defeated, thereby saving the energy that would be lost in needless aggression.
source: A key benefit to such reciprocation in such environments is the ability to downregulate a toxin once a competitor is defeated, thereby saving the energy that would be lost in needless aggression.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and interpretation presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells evolve to invest more in attacking their competitors when toxins are efficient at killing the competitor and/or the toxins persist stably in the environment.
source: Intuitively, we find that cells evolve to invest more in attacking their competitors when toxins are efficient at killing the competitor and/or the toxins persist stably in the environment (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in Table 1.

claim: A high benefit-to-cost ratio favours toxin use.
source: Toxin efficiency in our model is equivalent to the relative cost of toxin production, that is, we see a high benefit-to-cost ratio favours toxin use.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and is consistent with previous theory.

claim: This result is in line with previous theory, which has shown that the impact of toxin production on growth rate is critical for the evolutionary outcome.
source: This result is in line with previous theory, which has shown that the impact of toxin production on growth rate is critical for the evolutionary outcome (Bucci et al., 2011; Levin, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: For highly effective toxins, strains will engage in an arms race that escalates to the point where populations can go extinct.
source: For highly effective toxins, we find that strains will engage in an arms race that escalates to the point where populations can go extinct (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Such 'evolutionary suicide' is known from a wide range of conflict scenarios in biology.
source: Such 'evolutionary suicide' is known from a wide range of conflict scenarios in biology (Rankin and López-Sepulcre, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When nutrients are scarce, there is not enough energy to produce effective amounts of toxins.
source: When nutrients are scarce, there is not enough energy to produce effective amounts of toxins (Appendix 1—figure 3)
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Toxin benefit peaks at intermediate nutrient availability and decreases for higher nutrient levels.
source: However, we also find that toxin benefit peaks at intermediate nutrient availability and decreases for higher nutrient levels (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: When bacteria enter a competition at low density and resources are abundant, cells evolve to invest relatively little in toxin production; energy is instead better invested in rapid growth to win a competition by outgrowing other strains.
source: When bacteria enter a competition at low density and resources are abundant, there is a great potential for population expansion. Under these conditions, cells evolve to invest relatively little in toxin production; energy is instead better invested in rapid growth to win a competition by outgrowing other strains.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and interpretation.

claim: When growth potential is limited, cells benefit from investing in warfare, unless nutrients are too scarce to produce an effective toxin concentration.
source: In contrast, when growth potential is limited, cells benefit from investing in warfare, unless, as mentioned above, nutrients are too scarce to produce an effective toxin concentration.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and interpretation.

claim: Versions of each mode of regulation (nutrient sensing, quorum sensing, and toxin sensing) can stably invade all possible constitutive strategies.
source: Our analysis identifies versions of each mode of regulation that can stably invade all possible constitutive strategies (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: A well-regulated trait will outcompete an unregulated one unless maintaining a regulatory circuit is very costly.
source: This result is expected and confirms the basic intuition that – unless maintaining a regulatory circuit is very costly – a well-regulated trait will outcompete an unregulated one (Cornforth and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Shorter duration of competition selects for a higher initial investment in toxin production in order to ensure that enough toxin is made in the time that a strain has to compete.
source: This is true whether strains compete for a short or long duration, although shorter duration does select for a higher initial investment in toxin production in order to ensure that enough toxin is made in the time that a strain has to compete (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: For the great majority of cases, successful strains evolve to upregulate their attack after a delay, either based on the detection of low nutrients, high quorum, or high levels of the competitor's toxin.
source: For the great majority of cases, successful strains evolve to upregulate their attack after a delay, either based on the detection of low nutrients, high quorum, or high levels of the competitor's toxin (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: Toxin-based regulation not only upregulates toxin production after a delay, but also downregulates the toxin if the competitor is killed off.
source: A difference between nutrient and quorum sensing versus toxin-based regulation is that examples of the latter not only upregulate toxin production after a delay, they also downregulate the toxin if the competitor is killed off (Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Regulated strategies win by only making high levels of toxin at certain times, thereby saving energy relative to constitutive producers.
source: In each case, regulated strategies win by only making high levels of toxin at certain times, thereby saving energy relative to constitutive producers.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and interpretation.

claim: If toxin production is cost free, regulation will no longer be beneficial relative to constitutive production.
source: A corollary is that, if toxin production is cost free, regulation will no longer be benefitical relative to constitutive production.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the modeling framework.

claim: Assuming that there is some costs to toxin production, regulation is expected to be favoured by natural selection.
source: But, assuming that there is some costs to toxin production, regulation is expected to be favoured by natural selection.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the modeling results.

claim: When opponents have a single strategy (lowest diversity), the toxin sensing strategy is most efficient in terms of its final biomass produced.
source: When opponents have a single strategy (lowest diversity), the toxin sensing strategy is most efficient in terms of its final biomass produced (Figure 3a, left panel).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The toxin sensing strategy deals most effectively with diverse competitors.
source: Moreover, the toxin sensing strategy deals most effectively with diverse competitors (Figure 3a)
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Regression analysis shows a 2.5 times higher fitness for toxin sensing relative to the other strategies (p-value < 0.001).
source: with the regression analysis showing a 2.5 times higher fitness for toxin sensing relative to the other strategies (p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the modeling results.

claim: The success of the toxin sensing strategy is associated with the reliable activation of toxin production when sensing another toxin.
source: The success of the toxin sensing strategy is associated with the reliable activation of toxin production when sensing another toxin.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Quorum sensing activates toxin production during the competition but, in some cases, is defeated without being able to attack back.
source: Quorum sensing also activates toxin production during the competition but, in some cases, is defeated without being able to attack back.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: The nutrient-sensing strategy attacks first and then deactivates later when nutrients decrease.
source: The nutrient-sensing strategy, by contrast, attacks first and then deactivates later when nutrients decrease.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: The superiority of toxin sensing is robust across a range of parameters, including different toxin efficiencies, toxin loss rates, and nutrient concentrations.
source: This superiority of toxin sensing is robust across a range of parameters, including different toxin efficiencies, toxin loss rates, and nutrient concentrations (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: A strain that only engages in conflict when attacked will be best able to deal with a range of strategies that differ in their propensity and ability to attack.
source: There is a clear post hoc intuition to this result. A strain that only engages in conflict when attacked will be best able to deal with a range of strategies that differ in their propensity and ability to attack.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the modeling results.

claim: Toxin-sensing strains inactivate toxin production after a weak opponent is eliminated, thus employing the toxin efficiently.
source: More specifically, as seen in the last section, these strains inactivate toxin production after a weak opponent is eliminated, thus employing the toxin efficiently.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: For short competition times, while regulated strategies still outperform unregulated ones, the toxin sensing strategy fails to evolve a superior performance over the other modes of regulation.
source: For short competition times, while regulated strategies still outperform unregulated ones (Appendix 1—figure 5), the toxin sensing strategy fails to evolve a superior performance over the other modes of regulation (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 3b and Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: When competing with the same strategy, all strategies initially evolve to increase toxin production during the competition (finitial < finduced).
source: When competing with the same strategy, all strategies initially evolve to increase toxin production during the competition (finitial < finduced) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Strains responding to nutrient depletion initially produce near zero toxins (finitial = 0.05) until they activate toxin investment, at a level higher than the optimal fixed investment (evolved finduced = 0.50, while f* = 0.35).
source: More specifically, strains responding to nutrient depletion initially produce near zero toxins (finitial = 0.05) until they activate toxin investment, at a level higher than the optimal fixed investment (evolved finduced = 0.50, while f* = 0.35).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: Strains responding to quorum sensing invest in more toxin initially (finitial = 0.11) and also more when activated (finduced = 0.60).
source: In comparison, strains responding to quorum sensing invest in more toxin initially (finitial = 0.11) and also more when activated (finduced = 0.60).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: The quorum-sensing strategy is expected to be able to afford to invest more in toxin production because, unlike nutrient sensing, strains can reduce toxin investment again if biomass drops too low, thereby saving energy.
source: The quorum-sensing strategy is expected to be able to afford to invest more in toxin production because, unlike nutrient sensing, strains can reduce toxin investment again if biomass drops too low, thereby saving energy.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the modeling results.

claim: The toxin-sensing strategy invests near zero toxin at the start of the competition (finitial = 0.01) and responds very strongly if a competitor attacks (finduced = 0.73).
source: The toxin-sensing strategy is different again. It invests near zero toxin at the start of the competition (finitial = 0.01) and responds very strongly if a competitor attacks (finduced = 0.73).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: At evolutionary equilibrium (when toxin-sensing strains meet an identical toxin strategy), both remain passive and achieve a high biomass.
source: Interestingly, the corollary is that, at evolutionary equilbirum (when it will meet an identical toxin strategy), both remain passive and achieve a high biomass (Figure 4b center).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: This outcome has similarities to the success of 'tit-for-tat', a reciprocal cooperating strategy in the classic evolutionary game theory tournament of Axelrod and Hamilton, 1981.
source: This outcome has similarities to the success of 'tit-for-tat', a reciprocal cooperating strategy in the classic evolutionary game theory tournament of Axelrod and Hamilton, 1981.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous theoretical work.

claim: The evolution of a peaceful outcome is specific to the ability to reciprocate; we do not observe it for nutrient or quorum sensing.
source: The evolution of a peaceful outcome is specific to the ability to reciprocate; we do not observe it for nutrient or quorum sensing.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: There exists considerable variability in weapons and their regulation, even within a single species.
source: However, the model assumes that strains will only interact with other genotypes that are adopting similar strategies for warfare. This is far from guaranteed in bacteria as there exists considerable variability in weapons and their regulation, even within a single species (Mavridou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Microbial communities typically contain many strains and species.
source: Moreover, microbial communities typically contain many strains and species, suggesting again that a given strain has the potential to meet a diversity of competitors and strategies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microbial communities.

claim: In contests with other strategies, toxin-based regulation is a clear winner both for normal parameters and for sweeps that consider broad ranges of these parameters and a wide range of initial frequencies of the two strains.
source: Despite a great number of potential combinations (over two million different competitions), and with different sets of hyperparameters of the genetic algorithm, we again see a clear winner in toxin-based regulation, both for our normal parameters (Table 1, Figure 4c) and for sweeps that consider broad ranges of these parameters (Appendix 1—figure 8) and a wide range of initial frequencies of the two strains (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4c, Appendix 1—figure 8, and Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The success of toxin-based regulation in contests with other strategies does not come from an ability to avoid conflict and create peaceful outcomes.
source: Moreover, as for competition against unregulated strategies (Figure 3), the success of toxin-based regulation in contests with other strategies does not come from an ability to avoid conflict and create peaceful outcomes.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: The winning strategies are typically aggressive when they meet another strain and they only downregulate their toxins once an opponent is on its way to being eliminated.
source: Instead, the winning strategies are typically aggressive when they meet another strain and they only downregulate their toxins once an opponent is on its way to being eliminated (Figure 4d–f).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: For short competitions, there is no benefit in turning off an attack and the competitive benefit of reciprocity over other regulated strategies is lost.
source: And, as for competition against unregulated strategies, this ability to become passive is key to their success. For short competitions, there is no benefit in turning off an attack and the competitive benefit of reciprocity over other regulated strategies is lost (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 10.

claim: Bacteria use a wide variety of weaponry to harm other strains and species, which is typically under tight regulation.
source: Bacteria use a wide variety of weaponry to harm other strains and species, which is typically under tight regulation (Ghequire and De Mot, 2014; Granato et al., 2019; Stein, 2005; Michel-Briand and Baysse, 2002; Cascales et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: How bacteria employ these mechanisms of attack is central to understanding why a particular species or pathogen can invade and persist in communities, while others cannot.
source: How bacteria employ these mechanisms of attack is central to understanding why a particular species or pathogen can invade and persist in communities, while others cannot (Granato et al., 2019; Kommineni et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Toxin production is favoured under many conditions, particularly when toxins are effective and long-lasting and when the potential for population expansion is limited.
source: We find that toxin production is favoured under many conditions, particularly when toxins are effective and long-lasting and when the potential for population expansion is limited (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results presented in Table 1.

claim: The prevalence of aggressive strategies in our model is consistent with the widespread use of toxins by bacteria.
source: The prevalence of aggressive strategies in our model is consistent with the widespread use of toxins by bacteria (Granato et al., 2019), and the associated intensity of competition observed in experiments (Chao and Levin, 1981; Mavridou et al., 2018; Oliveira et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Well-regulated attacks can consistently outcompete strategies that lack regulation.
source: We also find that well-regulated attacks can consistently outcompete strategies that lack regulation (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The benefit of employing a toxin not only changes with different competitors but also within a single competition over time.
source: This is because the benefit of employing a toxin not only changes with different competitors but also within a single competition over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the modeling results.

claim: Regulation allows a strain to better tune its behaviour and follow the optimal investment at any given situation.
source: Regulation allows a strain to better tune its behaviour and follow the optimal investment at any given situation.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the modeling results.

claim: Across a diverse range of potential competitors, responding directly to incoming attacks is the most robustly successful strategy.
source: However, the three major classes of bacterial regulatory network are not always equivalent ways to control attacks. Across a diverse range of potential competitors, responding directly to incoming attacks is the most robustly successful strategy (Figures 3,4).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Our ODE model best reflects environments with limited spatial structure where cells of different genotypes are mixed together.
source: Within patches, our ODE model best reflects environments with limited spatial structure where cells of different genotypes are mixed together.
evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claim: Bacteria do display fine scale spatiogenetic structuring within their communities.
source: However, bacteria do also display fine scale spatiogenetic structuring within their communities (Nadell et al., 2016; Stacy et al., 2016; Krishna Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Our model has the potential to capture the outcome of competition at the interface of two strains, which is expected to be critical for success and persistence in such communities.
source: Here, our model has the potential to capture the outcome of competition at the interface of two strains, which is expected to be critical for success and persistence in such communities (Granato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a discussion of the model's potential applications, supported by a citation.

claim: In contrast to the detection of competitor's toxins, responses to quorum sensing and nutrient depletion may occur first in the middle of a patch of cells, where toxin production has the least benefit as toxin receivers are mainly clone-mates.
source: For example, in contrast to the detection of competitor's toxins, responses to quorum sensing and nutrient depletion may occur first in the middle of a patch of cells, where toxin production has the least benefit as toxin receivers are mainly clone-mates (Inglis et al., 2009; Wechsler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential spatial effects, supported by citations.

claim: Sensing incoming attacks through direct or indirect means should be a widespread way of regulating toxins and other modes of attack.
source: Our work predicts that sensing incoming attacks through direct or indirect means should be a widespread way of regulating toxins and other modes of attack.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Many bacteria upregulate attack mechanisms via stress responses that detect cell damage.
source: Some examples of reciprocation already exist. Many bacteria upregulate attack mechanisms via stress responses that detect cell damage (Cornforth and Foster, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is recent evidence of reciprocation between warring Escherichia coli strains where DNase protein toxins activate toxin production in competing strains via the SOS response to DNA damage.
source: This includes recent evidence of reciprocation between warring Escherichia coli strains where DNase protein toxins activate toxin production in competing strains via the SOS response to DNA damage (Mavridou et al., 2018; Krishna Kumar et al., 2021; Gonzalez et al., 2018; Granato et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Because many antimicrobials target the DNA of cells, sensing DNA damage is likely to be a relatively robust way to achieve reciprocity.
source: Because many antimicrobials target the DNA of cells (Janion, 2008; Gillor et al., 2008), sensing DNA damage is likely to be a relatively robust way to achieve reciprocity.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa senses incoming attacks via the type six secretion system (T6SS) of competitors, which delivers toxin via the molecular equivalent of a speargun.
source: But there are other mechanisms; Pseudomonas aeruginosa senses incoming attacks via the type six secretion system (T6SS) of competitors, which delivers toxin via the molecular equivalent of a speargun (Basler and Mekalanos, 2012; Basler et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon detecting an incoming attack via T6SS, a cell will activate its own T6SS in response.
source: Upon detecting an incoming attack, a cell will activate its own T6SS in response (Basler et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recent work suggests that a key benefit to reciprocation via the T6SS is the ability to save energy and only attack when necessary, alongside a benefit that comes from improved aiming which is specific to this mode of attack.
source: Consistent with our findings, recent work suggests that a key benefit to reciprocation via the T6SS is the ability to save energy and only attack when necessary, alongside a benefit that comes from improved aiming which is specific to this mode of attack (Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is evidence that bacteria may also detect and respond to incoming attacks via proxies such as the detection of lysate produced when surrounding cells are killed, or molecules that are made by an attacker alongside a toxin.
source: Finally, there is evidence that bacteria may also detect and respond to incoming attacks via proxies such as the detection of lysate produced when surrounding cells are killed (LeRoux et al., 2015a), or molecules that are made by an attacker alongside a toxin (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; LeRoux et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is evidence that bacterial toxins can be regulated via nutrient depletion and quorum sensing.
source: There is also evidence that bacterial toxins can be regulated via nutrient depletion and quorum sensing (Ghequire and De Mot, 2014; Cascales et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Our models of regulation by quorum or nutrients typically predict that attacks will evolve to be activated at high quorum or limited nutrients, which recapitulates the typical directionality of the regulation observed in nature.
source: Our models of regulation by quorum or nutrients typically predict that attacks will evolve to be activated at high quorum or limited nutrients, which recapitulates the typical directionality of the regulation observed in nature (Chandler et al., 2012; Fontaine et al., 2007; Inaoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: For short competition times, our model predicts that the three regulatory strategies are largely equivalent.
source: For short competition times, our model predicts that the three regulatory strategies are largely equivalent (Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 10.

claim: A short duration of competition between strains removes the benefit of decreasing toxin production once an attacker has been overcome.
source: A short duration of competition between strains removes the benefit of decreasing toxin production once an attacker has been overcome.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the modeling results.

claim: Under short competition conditions, the evolutionary path to one form of regulation may largely be determined by differences in costs for regulatory networks and which pre-existing regulatory systems are available for co-option.
source: Under these conditions, the evolutionary path to one form of regulation may largely be determined by differences in costs for regulatory networks and which pre-existing regulatory systems are available for co-option (Cotter and DiRita, 2000; Hockett et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results and supported by citations.

claim: Mechanisms to reciprocate attacks are particularly valuable in environments where warfare commonly leaves a victor unchallenged for a long time afterwards.
source: We predict, therefore, that mechanisms to reciprocate attacks are particularly valuable in environments where warfare commonly leaves a victor unchallenged for a long time afterwards.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: One of the clearest examples of reciprocation occurs in E. coli, which uses colicin toxins to displace other strains and persists for long periods within the mammalian microbiome.
source: Consistent with this, one of the clearest examples of reciprocation occurs in E. coli (Mavridou et al., 2018; Krishna Kumar et al., 2021; Granato et al., 2019), which uses colicin toxins to displace other strains and persists for long periods within the mammalian microbiome (Gillor et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
